name: Owners Path
subcategory: business owner planning and readiness tracking
tagline: A structured program and workspace for small business owners working toward a more valuable, less owner-dependent company.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Products in this space are usually two things bolted together: a software shell that holds assessments, scores, milestones and action items, and a methodology plus human advisors that tell you what the numbers mean. The shell is a one-session build: a few forms, a scoring function, a dashboard, a task list, an export button. The methodology is where the actual money goes, and copying someone's framework verbatim is both a legal question and a bad idea if you do not understand it. So you can build a very respectable personal owner-readiness tracker, then you are still the one deciding what to work on. If the value you want is accountability and an outside opinion, no amount of code delivers that.
coreLoopDIY: A local workspace where you define readiness categories, answer a periodic self-assessment, see scores trend over time, and track the action items you committed to.
requirements: Local machine to run it on
Your own framework for what to score and why
whatYouLose: The actual methodology: which questions matter, how they weight, what a bad score implies
Benchmarks against other companies, which is the only reason a score means anything
Advisor or coach accountability, the part that makes people finish things
Curated content, templates and sequencing of what to do first
Anyone to notice when you quietly stop logging in
moatNotes: The framework and any comparison benchmarks are the product; the CRUD around them is a weekend of typing.
whyPeopleStillPay: Owners pay for this category for the same reason they pay for a personal trainer instead of buying a barbell. The software is a prompt to do the work, and the work is uncomfortable, unscheduled and easy to defer forever. A self-built tracker has no opinion, no deadline and no one on the other end reading your answers. It is genuinely useful if you already know what you are working on and just want structure; it is useless as a substitute for someone telling you your business does not survive a month without you.
notes: The dashboard is trivial; knowing which twelve questions to put on it is not.
prompt:
Build a local-only "owner readiness" tracker as a single Next.js 15 app using the App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind, and SQLite through better-sqlite3. No auth, no cloud, no telemetry, single user on localhost.

Data model, stored in a local file data/app.db created on first run by a migration script:
- category: id, name, description, weight (integer 1 to 5), sort order
- question: id, category_id, text, help_text, scale_type ('1-5' or 'yes-no'), sort order
- assessment: id, taken_on (date), note
- answer: id, assessment_id, question_id, value (integer), comment
- action_item: id, title, detail, category_id nullable, due_date nullable, status ('open' | 'doing' | 'done'), created_at, completed_at nullable

Seed the database with five empty-ish starter categories the user is expected to rename (Financials, Operations, Team, Customers, Owner Dependence) and two placeholder questions each, clearly marked as placeholders. Do not ship any third-party framework content.

Screens:
1. /setup: CRUD for categories and questions, including weights and scale types. Inline editing, no modals.
2. /assessment/new: renders every question grouped by category, one screen, with a comment box per question and a save button. Saving creates an assessment plus its answers.
3. / (dashboard): overall weighted score out of 100 for the latest assessment, per-category scores as horizontal bars, a sparkline or simple SVG line chart of overall score across all assessments by date, and the three lowest-scoring categories called out as "work here next".
4. /history: table of past assessments, click one to view a read-only detail page with all answers and comments, plus a diff against the previous assessment showing which questions moved up or down.
5. /actions: kanban-lite list of action items in three columns by status, drag not required, a status dropdown is fine. Filter by category.

Scoring: normalize each answer to 0 to 1 ('1-5' maps 1 to 0 and 5 to 1; 'yes-no' maps 0 or 1), average within a category, then weight categories by their weight to produce the overall score. Put this in lib/score.ts with unit tests using node:test.

Also build: an export route that dumps everything to JSON, and an import route that accepts that JSON back. Include a make-style npm script "db:reset".

Explicitly out of scope: multi-user, invitations, advisor sharing, email reminders, benchmarks against other companies, PDF reports, any hosted deployment. Put nothing in .env except an optional PORT.

Finish with a README that states plainly: this app holds your answers, it does not know what good looks like, and the questions are yours to write.
